articles.title: Best AI Note-Taking Tools for Students
articles.author: Thanh Pham
articles.content:
If you want the short answer, Notion is the best AI note-taking tool for most students because it combines class notes, assignments, and AI study help in one place, and the student plan is unusually generous. AudioPen is better if you mainly want faster lecture capture, while Obsidian is stronger for students who care more about linking ideas than using built-in AI. The best choice depends on whether you need an all-in-one school system, better capture, or a deeper long-term knowledge base.
Quick Verdict
- Best all-around: Notion (free with .edu email). Best for lecture recording: AudioPen. Best for connected thinking: Obsidian. Best for zero-effort: Mem. Best for privacy: Reflect.
What You Need to Know
| Tool | Best For | Pricing | TL;DR | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Notion | Overall best | Free with .edu email | All-in-one for notes, tasks, and AI study help | 
| AudioPen | Lecture recording | Free / $29 one-time | Turns lecture recordings into structured notes automatically | 
| Obsidian | Connecting ideas | Free | Best for linking ideas across courses over four years | 
| Mem | Zero effort | Free / $12/month | Zero organizing — AI finds the connections for you | 
| Reflect | Privacy | $10/month | End-to-end encrypted notes, the most private option here | 
How I Evaluated This
I judged each tool by the specific student workflow it fits best — all-in-one organization, lecture capture, cross-course linking, zero-effort filing, or privacy — rather than treating them as interchangeable. Every price below was re-verified in July 2026.
1. Notion — Best All-Around Student Tool
Pricing: Free for students and educators (with .edu email)
Why it’s #1: Notion gives students a free workspace that handles notes, assignments, projects, and study planning in one place. With an .edu email, you get the full Personal Pro plan at no cost. That includes Notion AI for searching your notes, generating study guides, and summarizing long readings.
Student-specific setup:
- Course database: One entry per class with syllabus, notes, assignments, and grades
- Assignment tracker: Due dates, status, priority, linked to the relevant course
- Note-taking: Each lecture gets a page linked to its course
- Study guides: Ask Notion AI to generate a study guide from your notes before an exam
The all-in-one factor matters for students. Instead of notes in one app, tasks in another, calendar in a third… everything lives in Notion. When it’s time to study for finals, all your materials for every course are searchable in one place.
What I like for students:
- Free with .edu email (no budget concerns)
- AI search across all your notes (“What did we learn about photosynthesis?”)
- Database views for tracking assignments and grades
- Templates for common student needs (course tracker, reading log, study plan)
- Collaboration for group projects
What to watch out for:
- Setup takes time (spend an hour at the start of the semester)
- Can be overwhelming with too many features
- Limited offline access (need internet for full functionality)
2. AudioPen — Best for Lecture Recording
Pricing: Free (10 notes, 3 min each) / Prime $29 one-time / Premium $60/year
Why it’s here: AudioPen solves the lecture note-taking problem directly. Record the lecture (or just your thoughts after class), and AudioPen transcribes and rewrites it into structured notes. Not just a transcript… actual formatted notes with bullet points, summaries, and key points extracted.
The “Write Like Me” feature learns your note-taking style over time. After a few uses, the output matches how you’d organize the information yourself, just faster.
Student-specific uses:
- Record lectures and get structured notes immediately
- Record yourself summarizing what you learned (forces active recall)
- Convert rambling study session thoughts into organized study notes
- Multi-language support for international students
What I like for students:
- $29 one-time (Prime) is budget-friendly for students
- No subscription fatigue
- Works on phone, web, and desktop
- Style rewriting converts messy speech into clean notes
- Multi-language and accent handling
What to watch out for:
- Free tier is very limited (10 notes, 3 min each)
- Requires recording permission in lectures (check your school’s policy)
- Not a full note-taking system (pair with Notion or Obsidian for organization)
3. Obsidian — Best for Connected Thinking
Pricing: Free (personal and commercial use)
Why it’s here: Obsidian is built for connecting ideas. In a university setting where you’re studying multiple subjects that overlap (biology informs chemistry, history informs political science, psychology informs economics), the ability to link notes across courses is powerful.
The graph view shows a visual map of how your notes connect. Over four years, this becomes a personal knowledge base that maps your entire education. Students who use Obsidian well graduate with a searchable, connected library of everything they learned.
Student-specific uses:
- Link concepts across courses (evolution in biology → social Darwinism in history)
- Graph view reveals cross-disciplinary connections
- Daily notes for lecture capture
- Community plugins: flashcard generators, spaced repetition, citation managers
What I like for students:
- Completely free
- 2,000+ plugins for every need
- Files are plain Markdown (yours forever, any text editor can open them)
- Blazing fast search across thousands of notes
- Full offline access (study anywhere, no internet needed)
- Graph view is addictive and genuinely useful for connecting knowledge
What to watch out for:
- Steeper learning curve than Notion
- No built-in AI (requires community plugins)
- No native collaboration (hard for group projects)
- Sync between devices requires paid add-on ($4/month) or workaround
4. Mem — Best for Zero-Effort Organizing
Pricing: Free (25 notes/month) / Pro $12/month
Why it’s here: Some students hate organizing notes. They dump everything into one place and hope they can find it later. Mem is built for exactly this workflow.
No folders. No tags. No hierarchies. You capture notes, and Mem’s AI figures out how to organize them, surface connections, and find what you need later. For students who’ve tried and failed to maintain a note-taking system because the organizing part felt like a second homework assignment, Mem removes that friction entirely.
Student-specific uses:
- Dump lecture notes, reading highlights, and ideas in one stream
- AI surfaces related notes when you’re studying a topic
- Chat with your notes using GPT-4 (“Explain the connection between these two concepts”)
- Connected emails pipe in professor correspondence and assignment details
What I like for students:
- Zero organizational overhead
- AI finds connections you didn’t know existed
- Chat with your notes for exam prep
- Works for students who hate filing and organizing
What to watch out for:
- $12/month is real money for students
- Free tier (25 notes/month) is very limited
- Smaller ecosystem than Notion or Obsidian
- Trusting a startup with four years of notes is a risk
5. Reflect — Best for Privacy-Focused Students
Pricing: $10/month (14-day free trial, no free tier)
Why it’s here: Reflect is for students who care about data privacy. End-to-end encryption means even Reflect can’t read your notes. The AI understands your entire note graph (not just individual notes) and can auto-link related concepts.
Voice notes with Whisper transcription let you capture thoughts on the go. The speed-first design means the app opens instantly and never lags, even with thousands of notes.
Student-specific uses:
- Encrypted notes for sensitive research or personal journals
- Graph-aware AI suggests connections across courses
- Voice notes for quick capture between classes
- Kindle highlights import for reading-heavy courses
What I like for students:
- End-to-end encryption (privacy guaranteed)
- Graph-aware AI understands connections between notes
- Fast and minimal (no bloat, no feature overload)
- Voice notes with transcription for on-the-go capture
What to watch out for:
- $10/month with no free tier is the most expensive option
- No databases or task management (notes only)
- Smaller community and fewer integrations
- No collaboration features for group work
The Student Note-Taking Workflow
Here’s the workflow I’d recommend for students:
- During lectures: Record with AudioPen (phone in pocket or on desk). Take quick handwritten notes for key points.
- After lectures: Review AudioPen’s structured output. Paste into Notion or Obsidian with your own additions.
- During reading: Highlight in Kindle or web clipper. Highlights flow into your note system.
- Before exams: Ask Notion AI or Claude to generate study guides from your notes. Create flashcards. Quiz yourself.
- Long-term: Build connections between courses in Obsidian’s graph view or let Mem’s AI surface them automatically.
The $0 Student Stack
Every tool on this list has a free option:
- Notion: Free with .edu email (best free tier)
- Obsidian: Free (no restrictions)
- AudioPen: Free (limited to 10 notes)
- Claude free: For study guides and exam prep
- ChatGPT free: For research and explanation
- Anki: Free (spaced repetition flashcards)
Total cost: $0. A complete AI-powered study system without spending anything.
FAQ
Which one should I pick if I can only choose one?
Notion with your .edu email. It’s free, it handles notes and tasks, and the AI features help with studying. Add Obsidian (also free) if you want connected thinking on top.
Can I use AI to write my papers?
Using AI to research, outline, and understand material is fine and encouraged. Submitting AI-generated text as your own work is academic dishonesty at most institutions. Use AI as a study tool, not a ghost writer. Check your school’s specific AI policy.
Will these notes transfer after graduation?
Obsidian: Yes, your notes are plain Markdown files forever. Notion: Export is possible but not perfect. Mem and Reflect: Export available but format varies. If long-term portability matters, Obsidian is the safest choice.
What about Apple Notes or Google Keep?
Both work for quick capture. Neither has the AI features, linking, or database capabilities that make these tools powerful for serious studying. They’re fine as a capture inbox but not as your primary note system.
For how AI tools can accelerate your learning beyond note-taking, see How to Use AI to Learn Anything Faster.
Next Step

Notion, AudioPen, and Obsidian are among the top-rated AI-powered note-taking tools for students, offering specialized features for organization, lecture capture, and long-term knowledge management during the 2026 academic year.

### Key Points
- Notion provides a comprehensive, free workspace for students with a valid .edu email, integrating task tracking, databases, and AI-driven study assistance.
- AudioPen specializes in lecture capture by transcribing audio into structured, formatted notes, offering a one-time purchase option for students.
- Obsidian is a free, offline-first tool that uses a graph view to help students link concepts across different academic disciplines over time.

Selecting the right note-taking system can significantly improve academic efficiency by centralizing study materials and automating tedious organizational tasks. Students who leverage these AI tools effectively can create a more connected, searchable, and durable knowledge base to support their learning throughout their entire degree.

articles.title: Oops – Another Aussie State Just Forgot to Enforce Prime Minister Albanese’s Green Data Center Mandate
articles.author: Eric Worrall
articles.content:
Essay by Eric Worrall
Its a tough call – supporting the Federal Government’s renewable energy programme vs having an economic future.
Data centres are incompatible with renewable energy targets
Monday 27 July 2026
The Northern Territory government is backing plans for a $40 billion data centre industry, with several ‘hyper-scale’ AI data centre campuses to be built on land around 30 kilometres from Darwin.
These data centres would be powered by 3 GW of electricity generation, which in turn would be powered by gas from the NT’s Betaloo Basin.
The plan puts the NT government at odds with the federal government, which has drafted rules that would force data centres to power their operations with new renewable energy sources.
The issue is expected to come to a head at a meeting of energy ministers this week, with the Queensland government publicly opposed to the renewable-only proposal, given a lack of modelling and clarity over how the plan would work.
Data centres are incompatible with renewable energy targets:
The debate comes as Australia is on the verge of a major boom in data centre investment.
…
Read more: https://www.macrobusiness.com.au/2026/07/data-centres-are-incompatible-with-renewable-energy-targets/
The rebellion has spread from Queensland to the Northern Territory.
The economics driving this rebellion are simple – whoever breaks ranks with the federal green mandate gets to pull hundreds of billions of dollars of dollars of high tech investment, secure well paid jobs for university graduates, a construction industry boom, and a deluge of state tax revenue.
Whoever sticks with the Aussie federal government’s plan to try to force data centers to build renewables gets left in the dust.

The Northern Territory government is challenging federal renewable energy mandates by proposing a $40 billion data centre project powered by natural gas from the Beetaloo Basin near Darwin.

### Key Points
- The Northern Territory plans to build hyper-scale AI data centre campuses requiring 3 GW of electricity.
- Proposed facilities would rely on gas extraction from the Beetaloo Basin rather than renewable energy sources.
- Federal government rules currently aim to force new data centres to operate exclusively on renewable power.
- Queensland officials have joined the Northern Territory in opposing the federal mandate, citing a lack of economic modelling.
- State governments argue that prioritizing gas-powered infrastructure is essential to securing billions in high-tech investment and tax revenue.

### Why it Matters
This conflict highlights a growing tension between federal climate policy and state-level economic development strategies regarding the rapidly expanding AI data centre sector. The outcome of this dispute will determine whether Australia can attract major international technology investments or if strict renewable requirements will drive capital to more flexible jurisdictions.

- Bitcoin fell about 2.7 percent to roughly $63,200, extending losses across major cryptocurrencies as Asian equities, led by South Korea’s Kospi, sold off sharply.
- The U.S. Senate has delayed action on the closely watched CLARITY Act to focus on a Russia sanctions bill, likely pushing any vote on crypto regulatory legislation to next week before the Aug. 8 recess.
- Analysts say bitcoin tends to move with stocks when macro and interest-rate stress is high, and they expect volatility across asset classes around the Federal Reserve’s rate decision Wednesday and key U.S. data on Thursday.
Bitcoin 
BTC has fallen to $63,200 from nearly $65,000, a 2.7% decline that has spilled over into the broader crypto market and dragged down the likes of ether (ETH), XRP (XRP), solana (SOL), and others. The drop ends the brief resilience the market showed earlier Monday as shares in NVDA tanked on Wall Street.
The Senate has shelved the CLARITY Act to prioritize a Russia sanctions bill, making a vote on the much-awaited legislation, touted to deliver regulatory clarity and unlock massive institutional buying for digital assets, unlikely before next week. This leaves only the final days before the Aug. 8 recess.
Asian stocks cracked sharply, with South Korea’s Kospi index falling 10% to its lowest level since mid-April. The index has now dropped 25% from its mid-June peak. The latest decline featured steep losses in heavyweights such as Samsung and SK Hynix. "The market is falling out of love with chipmakers at the moment and that's been a big driver of the bull market in South Korea," InvestingLive wrote.
BTC has a history of tracking equity-market volatility, but the correlation is not as straightforward as widely perceived.
"BTC trades with equities when the stress is macro and [interest] rates-driven, and decouples when the stress is idiosyncratic to the equity market. An earnings-and-capital-expenditure debate is precisely that, so on this data the correlation is overstated," analysts at Bitfinex said in a note to CoinDesk.
Looking ahead, Wednesday and Thursday could significantly move the needle and add volatility across asset classes. The Fed decides interest rates on Wednesday, while Thursday brings key data.
"The Fed decides rates Wednesday, with Core PCE and GDP following immediately Thursday. That makes Wednesday–Thursday the week's highest-volatility window for U.S. rate repricing," Dessislava Ianeva, analyst at Nexo, said.

articles.title: Nvidia, Tech Giants Launch AI Safety Initiative
articles.author: BeauHD
articles.content:
wiredmikey shares a report from SecurityWeek: Nvidia and a large group of technology, cybersecurity, and enterprise software companies have launched new initiative aimed at developing and sharing open source tools, models, and techniques for securing AI systems and agents. The new Open Secure AI Alliance aims to give defenders more open tools for testing, auditing and protecting AI models and agents. Nvidia points to the recent security incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, noting that when closed AI tools could not differentiate between attackers and defenders and blocked forensic work, Hugging Face used the open-weight GLM 5.2 model on its own systems to review over 17,000 actions and contain the breach. "The right response is not to deny defenders access to capable open systems. It is to pair openness with strong safeguards, clear rules against malicious misuse, rigorous evaluation and rapid remediation. In cybersecurity, the safer path is the one that gives more defenders the ability to test, verify and strengthen the systems on which society relies," Nvidia said.
 
Thanks to longtime Slashdot reader SphericalCrusher for also sharing the news.

Nvidia and a coalition of technology firms have launched the Open Secure AI Alliance to develop open-source tools for testing, auditing, and protecting artificial intelligence systems from threats.

### Key Points
- The Open Secure AI Alliance focuses on creating shared resources to help defenders identify and mitigate vulnerabilities in AI models and agents.
- Nvidia advocates for open-weight systems, citing a recent incident where Hugging Face used the GLM 5.2 model to analyze 17,000 actions during a breach.
- The initiative emphasizes that open access to security tools allows defenders to verify system integrity more effectively than relying solely on closed-source software.
- Participating companies aim to establish rigorous evaluation standards and rapid remediation protocols to prevent malicious misuse of AI technology.

### Why it Matters
This initiative represents a strategic shift toward transparency in AI security, prioritizing collaborative defense over the limitations of proprietary, closed-source systems. By standardizing open-source auditing tools, the alliance aims to improve the resilience of critical infrastructure against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

articles.title: Chipmakers fall in US and Asia as AI jitters rattle investors
articles.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
articles.content:
- Published
Shares in major chip firms have fallen sharply in the US and Asia as a sell-off in artificial intelligence-related stocks deepened.
Trading on South Korea's benchmark Kospi index was paused temporarily on Tuesday morning after sliding by 8%. It fell further after the 20-minute halt was lifted, closing 10.8% lower.
The slump was led by technology firms, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both falling by more than 13%.
It comes after AI chip giant Nvidia fell by 5% in New York on Monday, meaning it lost its position as the world's most valuable listed company to Apple.
The tech-heavy Kospi has been halted multiple times so far this year under a stock market mechanism known as a circuit breaker, which is designed to calm panic selling.
The index had more than doubled from the start of the year to mid-June but has since lost around a third of its value.
In recent months stock market trading has been particularly volatile in South Korea as it has attracted large numbers of retail investors.
On Monday, US-listed shares in SK Hynix fell by 7.5% to well below the $149 (£112.11) offer price when it made a record-breaking debut on the Nasdaq on 9 July.
Japan's Nikkei 225, which is also dominated by tech companies, closed almost 4% lower.
Jane Sydenham, investment director at investment manager Rathbones, said the Asian market slump came after "phenomenal rises" over the last few months.
She said the Korean market in particular is "very concentrated" with a lot of investment in Samsung and SK Synix, both of which fell sharply.
In addition, a lot of Korean investors buy stocks with debt, which "exaggerates the movements when we get a correction like this".
Sydenham said the sell-off was triggered by Nvidia, whose shares fell on Monday after the Wall Street Journal reported that it is in talks to provide around $250bn for OpenAI as part of a massive data-centre project.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia and OpenAI for comment.
The decline allowed Apple to overtake Nvidia as the world's most valuable company after the iPhone maker rose by about 25% this year.
Cheng Chye Hsern, head of investments at wealth manager Providend, said Apple is one the few tech firms "not taking part in the AI race".
He said this makes the stock appealing to investors who are concerned about the billions its rivals are spending on data centres.
Sydenham said AI spending among tech firms is "something that's been testing investors' nerves on and off in the last couple of months".
"Is it going to earn a proper return in the future? That's what investors are worried about."
Jun Bei Liu, the founder of investment firm Ten Cap, told the BBC there are also worries about increasing competition from China.
As such, she said investors are "taking some profit off the table" but are likely to reinvest in these stocks after the US holiday season, she said.
Shares in China's biggest memory chip maker, ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), soared by nearly 470% as they made their debut in Shanghai on Monday.
The company said said it plans to use most of the proceeds from the initial public offering (IPO) to boost production and carry out more research and development.
CXMT manufactures dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips that power AI data centres, mobile phones, PCs, tablets and other devices.
The big European stock markets all shrugged off the AI spending concerns when they opened on Tuesday.
The UK's FTSE 100 index, France's Cac 40, and the German Dax 40 have relatively less exposure to AI and were all around 0.6% up a couple of hours after trading began.

Global stock markets experienced a sharp sell-off in artificial intelligence-related shares, led by significant declines in South Korean tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix following Nvidia's recent losses.

### Key Points

articles.title: 5 Disadvantages Of Using Video Doorbells
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (Suzanne Bonnett)
articles.content:
5 Disadvantages Of Using Video Doorbells
Video doorbells were quick to become one of the most ubiquitous smart home devices on the market. From the suburbs to city apartment complexes, it seems like almost every front door now sports a camera-toting rectangle. They promise peace of mind, after all, letting you screen visitors from the comfort of your couch or keep a watchful eye on your porch while you're away from home. But while these devices offer a layer of convenience and security that's hard to say no to, they're far from flawless and actually have several downsides.
To clarify, these doorbells are not inherently bad investments, especially if you opt for a nicer 2K video doorbell. For many homeowners, they quickly pay for themselves by making it easier to catch a package thief or see when the kids get home from school. But as these devices have evolved, so, too, have the unforeseen complications that can come with mounting an always-on camera to the front of your house.
While video doorbells offer an easy and fairly straightforward upgrade in your home's security, they bring with them some concerns that manufacturers don't exactly advertise, like creeping privacy issues and annoying technical hurdles. Ultimately, relying on a smart doorbell means making a few noteworthy compromises. So if you're thinking about adding one to your smart home ecosystem, here are the biggest disadvantages of using video doorbells worth your consideration.
Privacy problems extend far beyond your property lines
During the early days of the smart home tech boom, nobody was thinking much about the ethical implications of smart doorbells. Everyone was sold on being able to see who was at the door, and that was that. Unfortunately, the reality of strapping an always-on, high-definition camera to your front door is that it inevitably captures much more than your own property.
Depending on where you live and how your front porch is oriented, video doorbells can likely record your neighbors' daily movements, pedestrians walking their dogs, and every car that drives down the street. This casual-seeming surveillance net has raised huge privacy problems over the last few years. While you might feel safer, your neighbors may not appreciate being unknowingly recorded every time they step out to check the mail. Beyond local neighborhood dynamics, however, there are far bigger concerns regarding how the companies that manufacture these doorbells handle your video data.
Big company names like Ring have faced enormous backlash for sharing user footage with law enforcement agencies without getting explicit user consent or a warrant from the people who own those video doorbells. Furthermore, because these devices are internet-connected, they'll always carry the ever-lurking risk of being hacked. A compromised video doorbell can give malicious actors direct access to the audio and video feeds of your family's daily routine, turning what was supposed to be a private security device for your family into a potent surveillance tool working against you.
Reliability is largely at the mercy of your Wi-Fi quality
A traditional, old-school doorbell is delightfully simple: you press the button, the circuit closes, and the chime rings to alert you of a visitor. And better yet, it works every single time, without fail, for decades. If you look at some of the best smart home gadgets on the market, many try (and often fail) to match that fundamental reliability, and video doorbells are no exception. The gaping issue here is that these devices are dependent on the strength and stability of your home's Wi-Fi network.
This might not seem like a massive hurdle on the surface, but your front door is one of the toughest areas in your home for wireless signals to pierce through. Thick exterior walls, metal doors, brick facades, and the like can all combine to create a dead zone right where you need connectivity the most. So when the Wi-Fi signal drops or fluctuates, so, too, does your video doorbell's performance. You might get a notification that someone is at the door, but when you open the app, all you can see is a spinning loading wheel or a heavily pixelated (and, thus, useless) feed. And by the time the video finally resolves, the person has already walked away.
While that's fine for handling door-to-door salesmen, it's more than annoying when it's a friendly neighbor or repairman. Additionally, battery-powered models suffer drastically in extreme weather; both freezing winter and scorching summer temperatures can shorten a doorbell's battery capacity, leaving you completely blind until you unmount, recharge, and remount it.
Camera and hardware limitations leave behind blind spots
As camera lenses and sensors have improved, manufacturers have boasted about ultra-wide viewing angles and crisp 4K resolutions for their video doorbells. While these devices can effortlessly capture a sweeping view of your front yard, physics still gets in the way of complete security. A major downside of these devices is their fixed position, which can create blind spots. No matter how advanced the lens is, a camera mounted at standard doorbell height is going to have those blind spots. That's something that can render them less than effective at the one thing they're supposed to be doing: letting you see what's happening around your front door and yard.
The most common victim of this shortcoming is delivered packages sitting on your porch. Delivery drivers are known for placing boxes on the ground right below the camera's field of view or tucking them behind a nearby planter to hide them from the street. Because the camera on these doorbells looks outward rather than down, package thieves can potentially sneak in and swipe your deliveries without ever really showing their face on camera.
Some newer models have even added secondary downward-facing cameras to combat this exact issue. The only remaining issue is at night, as there's lower visibility; even infrared sensors used for night vision have the potential to wash out an image and make it hard to see much detail, let alone faces beyond a few feet. It's a frustrating hardware limitation that leaves obvious gaps in your home security.
The hidden costs of often-mandatory usage subscriptions
Although there are several security cameras that don't require a subscription, video doorbells definitely lie within the realm of software-as-a-service models that do. Regardless of whether you stayed budget-friendly with a sub-$100 video doorbell or you splurged on a higher-end $250 model, it's reasonable to expect it to be fully functional right out of the box. However, this initial hardware purchase ends up being more like a down payment for your video doorbell: for the most part, unlocking their full utility almost always ends up with you getting strongarmed into paying a monthly or yearly subscription fee.
Though there are subscription-free doorbells, they often have limited functionality, in comparison. They might still send you a live alert when someone rings the bell, but they won't let you do anything like save or review recorded video clips. So if your motion sensor goes off in the middle of the night and you sleep through the notification, you can't check the app the next morning to see what happened; that footage is instantly gone unless you are paying the company to store it in the cloud so you can see it later on.
Beyond that, some brands lock their most useful intelligent features (like the ability to tell between a human being and a passing car) behind these paywalls, as they typically need cloud computing to work. Over the lifespan of the device, you'll easily end up spending more money on the accompanying subscription than you ever did on the video doorbell hardware itself.
Notification fatigue and false alerts reduce usefulness
Normally, a security device is supposed to help you feel safe and calm, but an overly sensitive video doorbell can quickly become an all-day source of anxiety and annoyance. The final major disadvantage of installing one of these devices is the sheer amount of notifications they can send you. While you absolutely want to know when someone's at your door, it's possible to adjust the sensitivity and zones for motion sensor alerts, but getting them dialed in just right can be tough, as a video doorbell's default alert sensitivity can be too high and end up sending you a bunch of false alerts.
This might mean your phone buzzes every time a car drives by in your neighborhood, or your tree moves in the wind on a sunny yet breezy day. The constant stream of pings makes it easy to end up with notification fatigue. After jumping to check your phone for the billionth time just to see a stray cat walking across your lawn, you might start ignoring alerts altogether. And once you stop paying attention to the notifications, the device loses almost all of its preventative security value.
Though you can spend hours tweaking the sensitivity sliders and drawing activity zones in your smart doorbell's companion app, finding that perfect balance between missing real events and being spammed by false ones might feel impossible. Swiping away incoming alerts from fatigue can all but render your doorbell an expensive, useless gadget. And given that video doorbells can last several years, that's a lot of money out of your pocket you're potentially handing away.
articles.summary:
While video doorbells offer convenient home security, users must navigate significant drawbacks including privacy concerns, technical reliability issues, hardware blind spots, recurring subscription costs, and frequent false motion alerts.

### Key Points
- Privacy risks include the unauthorized recording of neighbors and potential data sharing between manufacturers like Ring and law enforcement agencies.
- Wi-Fi dependency often leads to connectivity dead zones, causing delayed notifications or pixelated video feeds during critical moments.
- Fixed camera angles create blind spots that frequently obscure packages left on porches, rendering them vulnerable to theft.
- Most devices require ongoing monthly or yearly subscription fees to access essential features like cloud storage and advanced motion detection.
- Excessive false alerts from wind or passing traffic can cause notification fatigue, leading users to ignore the device entirely.

### Why it Matters
Video doorbells represent a long-term commitment to both recurring costs and potential security vulnerabilities that extend beyond the home. Understanding these trade-offs is essential for consumers to determine if the convenience of smart monitoring outweighs the risks to personal privacy and hardware reliability.

articles.title: PSA: T-Mobile is down, iPhones showing ‘SOS’ mode
articles.author: Chance Miller

Update #3, 8:33 p.m. PT: T-Mobile says it has “fully restored service for all customers and sincerely apologize for the difficulties to those who experienced network impacts.”
Update #2, 4:15 p.m.PT: In a statement to 9to5Mac, a T-Mobile spokesperson said:
“Our teams are actively working the reports of technical challenges impacting some customers. Any service impacts are in the process of being resolved and are our highest priority. We know how critical it is to stay connected, and every available resource is focused on resolving this as quickly as possible.”
Update #1, 3 p.m. PT: Some T-Mobile users report that service is returning to their iPhones. Others, however, say the outage is ongoing.
T-Mobile is down across the United States, and many iPhone users are seeing “SOS” in their device’s status bar. Here’s everything you need to know about today’s T-Mobile outage.
T-Mobile is down, iPhones in ‘SOS’ mode
Data aggregated by Downdetector shows that the T-Mobile outage began right around 4 p.m. ET/1 p.m. PT. The outage appears to be widespread, with users across the United States reporting problems with their service.
A thread on Reddit has amassed thousands of complaints from T-Mobile subscribers who say they are unable to place calls, send texts, and use cellular data on their devices. There are also thousands of complaints from T-Mobile users on other social networks.
Several of us here at 9to5Mac are also impacted by the T-Mobile outage and are unable to use any cellular networking features on our iPhones.
Top comment by Ed Cory
My iPhone was the only one out of four in my family that wasn't working. I was actively texting my wife, network went out at 3:21pm central in the STL greater area. Weird.
I had also received a message about a "30 day 20GB Hotspot Data Pass expiring in 1 hour" at 8:33, then another saying it was then expired at 9:33. I didn't sign up for any such thing. When I went to my phone's Cellular Plan area during the outage, it said '20GB Hotspot Data Pass'. So I wonder if someone thought they were being clever and "just disabled the cancelled plans", but overwrote the cellular plans assigned to our devices.
iPhone users affected by the outage are seeing the “SOS” icon in their device’s status bar. This indicates there is no network connectivity whatsoever. If you see this on your iPhone, it means T-Mobile is down in your area due to the outage. You can, however, still make emergency calls.
As of right now, T-Mobile has not commented on the outage and it’s unclear when it will be fixed. it doesn’t appear that other carriers, including Verizon and AT&T, are also down.

T-Mobile has fully restored cellular service across the United States following a widespread network outage that left many iPhone users unable to place calls or access mobile data.

### Key Points
- The outage began around 4 p.m. ET on the affected date, causing widespread connectivity issues for subscribers nationwide.
- Impacted iPhone users reported seeing an "SOS" icon in their status bars, indicating a total loss of cellular network connectivity.
- Downdetector and social media platforms, including Reddit, recorded thousands of user complaints regarding the inability to send texts or use data.
- T-Mobile confirmed the resolution of the technical challenges and issued a formal apology to customers for the service disruption.
- Competitor networks, including Verizon and AT&T, were not reported to be affected by the technical issues impacting T-Mobile.

### Why it Matters
Reliable cellular connectivity is essential for modern communication, and widespread outages highlight the vulnerability of mobile infrastructure to technical failures. This incident underscores the critical dependence consumers have on carrier stability for both personal communication and emergency services.
